title: Why Cities Are Hotter Than the Countryside

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about a phenomenon that affects most large cities, the urban heat island effect. In simple terms, it means that a city is warmer than the countryside around it. On a calm summer night, the centre of a big city can be up to five degrees warmer than the surrounding fields, and that difference has serious consequences for health, energy use and even sleep.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: I'll begin with the main causes, then move on to some proposed solutions, and finally I'll say something about why progress has been so slow. There are three main causes, and I'll take them in turn.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The first is the surface material. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb far more heat from the sun than grass or soil, and they release it slowly afterwards. A black road can be thirty degrees hotter than a lawn next to it at midday.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The second cause is the lack of vegetation. Trees do not only provide shade. They also release water vapour through their leaves, and this process takes heat out of the air, much as sweating cools our skin. Replace a wooded area with a car park and you lose both effects at once.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: The third cause is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings on both sides of a narrow street form what planners call a street canyon. During the day, sunlight bounces between the walls and stays trapped. At night, the problem is worse, because the heat has nowhere to go. The buildings block the sky, so warmth that would normally escape upwards is held in the streets.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Now, many people assume that air conditioning is the main culprit. That is partly true, since all that machinery pumps warm air outside. But when researchers compared different districts, the effect of surface materials turned out to be considerably larger. So air conditioning is a contributing factor rather than the root cause.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Let's turn to solutions. One popular idea is to paint roofs white so that they reflect sunlight. It's an appealing idea, and it does work on individual buildings. But I think it's slightly oversimplified, because white surfaces can also reflect glare down into the street, and they do nothing to help with the shortage of trees.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Another option is the green roof, which is a roof covered in plants. The benefits are real. They cool the building, absorb rainwater and provide a home for insects. Even so, the installation is expensive, so I suspect they will remain rare unless governments offer financial support.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: A recent study in a European city offered a surprising lesson. The researchers expected the biggest cooling effect near the largest parks. In fact, the strongest cooling came from many small green spaces spread across the district, because each one cooled the streets immediately around it. That suggests that quantity and distribution may matter more than sheer size.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: To sum up, we already know how to reduce urban heat. The real difficulty is that responsibility is divided between many different organisations, so the obstacle is coordination rather than technology. Cities that plan their trees, roofs and streets together are likely to have a distinct advantage, and I'd argue that is where future research should focus.
